full_judgment:
These two Rules are directed against two orders of the learned Munsif in two different proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Munsif rejected the application for addition of parties in each of the proceedings. 

 2. One Ruhul Amin Sardar filed an application under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for correction of record of right in respect of the properties mentioned in the schedule to the application. It is Khatian No. 2184 Plot No. 2594 measuring 11.97 acres. This land has been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 in the name of the Deputy Commissioner. In this application Bangladesh has been impleaded as opposite party No. 1 and Sailuddin Sardar, Golam Rabbani and Ramjan Ali, the three brothers of Ruhul Amin have been impleaded as opposite parties 2 to 4 (preform) The allegations made in the petition are that the land in question originally belonged to Roy Harendra Nath and others in khas under the anent-merit and the petitioner Ruhul Amin and his three other brothers took settlement of Plot No. 2594 at a rental of Rs 90-8 annas in 1332 B S. and continued to possess the same along with other lands. The said lands have been wrongly recorded in the impugned current khatian. 

 3. Sailuddin Sardar Golam Rabbani and Ramjan Ali as petitioners filed a similar petition under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on the allegations inter alia that they have tenancy in respect of 12.71 acres of land which has been recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 1 in the name of Deputy Commissioner. Reliefs have been prayed in the same terms as in the case of Ruhul Amin Sardar. In this case Bangladesh has been impeladed as opposite party No. 1 and Ruhul Amin has been impleaded as opposite party No. 2 (proforma) and on this application Miscellaneous case No. 244 of 1973 (143) was started. 

 4. The Bangladesh appeared in both the cases and filed written objection. Thereafter the order sheets indicates various other developments of the proceedings. Upon application of the instant petitioners for addition of parties under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned Munsif heard the parties and rejected the application in both the cases. According to the learned Munsif, the application was not maintainable and Tenancy Act does not provide for addition of opposite parties. Against the aforesaid order of the learned Munsif the instant Rules were obtained. It appears that an order has been recorded for analogous bearing of, the two Rules. Accordingly, both the Rules are taken up together for bearing. 

 6. Mr. M.B. Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties in both the Rules, contends that section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Order I rule 10 have no application in the special provisions for correction of record of right under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. According to Mr. Rahman the applications for addition of parties are misconceived and not maintainable. It is, therefore, necessary to consider what section 143A stands for. It runs as follows: 

 8. Assuming, as Mr. Shahid contends, that in the instant proceeding Order 1 rule 10 shall apply, evidently, sub-rule (1) has no manner of application. In terms of sub-rule (2) the court jurisdiction to add a party whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all questions involved in the suit. In the background of the above provision, can it be said that section 143A contemplates a proceeding of such nature or is a proceeding which is deemed to be a suit where all questions involved in the suit or proceeding may be effectually and completely adjudicated upon ? Obviously section 143A contemplates a summary power to be exercised by the Civil Court within the prescribed limits. The purpose of introducing this special provision is "correcting mistakes". The special provisions made in section 143A are intended for a definite and limited purpose. The legislative intent is clearly available from the language used in sub-section (I) of section 143A. Sub-section (2) contains the statutory fiction for extending the meaning of the terms "application" and "order" which they do not in reality imply but the statute requires them to be as such. Sub-section (2) does not enlarge the scope, object and purpose of sub-section (1). The procedure prescribed in the subsequent sub-sections is intended for the purpose of carrying out the purpose and object of "correcting mistakes". Sub-section (13) indicates that relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall mutatis mutandis apply for the purpose of an application, appeal, review, revision and consequence of non-appearance. It is difficult to conceive that the Code of Civil Procedure has been made applicable in its terms and as a whole. Therefore, the contention of Mr. Shahid that section 143A. not bring exhaustive and in the absence of provision for addition of opposite parties there in, the provisions of Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall apply on the strength of section 141 of the Code does not appear to stand on a sound footing within the meaning and scope of, section 143A of the State Acquit sit ion and Tenancy Act. Thus, the application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. does not appeal to be maintainable. The learned Munsif in this behalf appears to have rightly rejected the petition for addition of parties. 

 9. Mr. Shahid has next contended that the applicants are some of the members of the public and they came to protect a public right in the nature of easement in respect of the suit land. The scope of enquiry under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act relates to correcting mistakes in respect of an entry or omission of entry in the record-of-rights prepared or revised and finally published under Chapter IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, the right of the applicants, if any, cannot be adjudicated in the instant proceeding. The applicants not being parties can never be affected by an order passed in the proceeding. According to Mr. Shahid the members of the public have been enjoying a right recognised by the Government. It does not appear that the Government has denied the right of the public The alleged right of easement is sought to be confirmed by the applicants In the instant proceeding but this question is absolutely beyond the scope of investigation under section 143A. 

 11. It must, however, be pointed out that section 143A is not intended to be misused in the way it has been sought to be done in the instant applications. In paragraph 5 of the respective petition, certain prayers have been made in declaratory form with regard to title of the petitioner or petitioners. It does not appear that section 143A contemplates such a relief as prayed for in the two cases. It further appears that the trial court proceeded to deal with the two cases as if these are suits for title. It appears that an Advocate Commissioner was appointed and he submitted certain report. Could the question, be decided within the scope of section 143A. The reply evidently is in the negative. Caution should be taken by the Court below not to encourage adjudication of disputed title and possession under the garb of a proceeding under section 143A. A complete end effectual adjudication with regard to title and possession must be left open for properly constituted suit. A proceeding under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act should not be allowed to transcend its limited scope expressly provided by statute itself. The legislative intent and purpose should not be overlooked. It is not necessary for me to express my views on the applications under section 143A, since they have to be disposed of by the trial court according to law. The observation made by me are meant for guidance of the learned Muncie who is however free to dispose of the matters on consideration of necessary questions and according to law. 

 For the reasons stated above there is no ground for interference under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
